title: Day 85 · Week 12, Day 1 — Brain: the first preference — the right arm at ten weeks, the thumb at fifteen, sixty of sixty, the spinal cord that picks a side before the brain, the one in ten, and the left-handers who didn't die young
summary: The Brain episode on handedness, which starts long before the first crayon. At 10 weeks 85% of 72 fetuses moved the right arm more than the left, at an age when the brain probably isn't driving the arms (Hepper 1998). From 15 weeks most fetuses suck the right thumb, independent of position (Hepper 1991), and in the one follow-up, 60 of 60 right-thumb-suckers were right-handed at 10–12 years and 10 of 15 left-thumb-suckers were left-handed (Hepper 2005). The preference may begin in the spinal cord, with epigenetically regulated left–right gene expression (Ocklenburg 2017, five fetuses). Left-handedness prevalence is 9.3–18.1% depending on definition, best estimate 10.6%, with cultural pressure lowering observed rates (Papadatou-Pastou 2020); genes explain ~25% of variation and the shared family environment none (Medland 2006, 21,127 twin pairs); 41 loci for left-handedness and 7 for ambidexterity in 1.77 million people (Cuellar-Partida 2021); blood methylation captures little (Odintsova 2022). The old claim that left-handers die younger was an artefact of switched children (Salive 1993). Verdict: nothing to optimise; let the hand choose.
action: In the pregnancy file's 'First weeks' section, add one line: 'Hand: let them choose. Don't move the crayon.' At the next scan, watch the arms — the preference is already there.
